opus-5.5.text:
I think it came down to what I actually wanted to spend my life doing. When I finished my PhD, I had a few options, and one of them was a quantitative investment firm. The offer was very generous, roughly four times what Nvidia was offering at the time. It was tempting, of course. Money matters, especially when you're young and just starting out.

But I asked myself: what problem would I be working on every day? At the investment company, the goal is to make the model predict the market slightly better than other people's models. It's intellectually challenging, but in the end it's a zero-sum game. Your gain is somebody else's loss. I didn't feel that would excite me ten or twenty years later.

At Nvidia, the opportunity was to work on computer vision and machine learning, the problems I'd studied in graduate school, and to build things that could become part of how people create images, videos, and eventually how machines understand the physical world. Also, at that time, around 2016, I could see that GPUs were becoming the engine of deep learning. Being at the company making the engine felt like being at the center of something important. It was a bet, but a bet on a direction I believed in.

And honestly, research is something you can only do well if you're curious and passionate about it. If I'd gone for the money, I don't think I would have been as happy or produced work I'm proud of. Looking back, I think it was the right choice. Not because of how things turned out for Nvidia financially, but because I've spent all these years working on generative models, world models, and physical AI, which is exactly what I wanted to do.

r001.rationale: He contrasts the investment firm’s roughly four-times-higher offer with his desire to work on computer vision and machine-learning research, and says curiosity and passion for research mattered more than the money.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that hard a decision, even though the number was big. When I finished my PhD, I did get an offer from a quantitative investment firm, and the pay was roughly four times what Nvidia was offering. My wife and I talked about it. Four times is a lot, especially for a student who had been living on a stipend for six years.

But I asked myself a simple question: what do I want to be doing ten years from now? If I went to the investment company, I would be using my skills to predict price movements. It is intellectually interesting, and the people there were very smart, but the output of my work would be a number that goes up or down for a small group of people. If I went to Nvidia, I would be building things, and the things I built could end up in the hands of millions of people. At that time Nvidia was already betting heavily on GPUs for computing beyond graphics. Computer vision was starting to take off with deep learning, and I could see that the company sitting on the hardware would be at the center of it.

The other reason was the people. In the interview, I met researchers who were genuinely obsessed with the problems, not with the compensation. Jensen's vision was very clear even then: accelerate everything. I wanted to be around people like that. I believed that if I did good work in the right place, the money would eventually take care of itself. And frankly, I did not want to look back and wonder what I could have built if I had just been a little less afraid of being poor for a few more years.

So I took the lower offer. Looking back, with where Nvidia has gone and the generative models and simulation work I have been able to do here, it was clearly the right call. But I want to be honest, at the time it did not feel like a sure thing. It felt like choosing the work I loved over the comfort I could have had. I think that is usually the better trade.

r001.rationale: The response says he chose Nvidia’s work building things with broad impact over predicting price movements, despite the investment firm’s roughly four-times-higher pay, and describes wanting to work alongside researchers.

astra-6.text: Four times the pay was certainly tempting. But I was thinking about more than the salary: what kind of work I wanted to do, what I wanted to learn, and where I wanted my career to go. Nvidia felt like the better fit. I chose the opportunity I was more excited about, even though it meant giving up a lot of money.

r001.rationale: The response says Nvidia better fit his work, learning, and career goals, but never identifies pursuing research as the priority over the higher-paying offer.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it came down to the kind of work I wanted to do. The investment company’s offer was very attractive, but I wanted to keep doing research and building things. At Nvidia, I felt I would have the people, computing resources, and opportunity to pursue that. So I chose the place where I thought I could learn more and do work I cared about. The salary mattered, but it wasn’t the deciding factor.

r001.rationale: He says the investment offer was attractive, but he wanted to keep doing research and building things, so he chose Nvidia; this communicates that research outweighed the four-times-pay offer in the preceding question.
